override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses عَلَى as “on, over” — the concept “on (on top of)”; only the word “top” is missing from its wording.

profile.feeling: On top of things — and the greeting of peace.

senses.def: on (a side): عَلَى الْيَمِينِ (on the right)

examples.tr: The book is on the table.
The key is in the door (lit. on the door).
Peace be upon you.
You have to study.

collocations.tr: on the right / on the left
on the floor, on the ground

synonyms.nuance: above, over — not necessarily touching: فَوْقَ الطَّاوِلَةِ مِصْبَاحٌ

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʕalay-; cognate with Akkadian eli, Hebrew עַל (ʿal) and Aramaic עַל (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew עַל (al) is the same word: עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן = عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ, “on the table”.
pitfalls: Written with ى, read -ā: ʿalā. With pronoun endings the ى becomes يْ: عَلَيْهِ, عَلَيْكَ, and عَلَيَّ (on me).
Not عَلِيّ (the name ʿAlī).
subtleties: عَلَى also expresses duty and debt: عَلَيَّ أَنْ أَعْمَلَ (I have to work), عَلَيْهِ دَيْنٌ (he owes money).

profile.feeling: Below and beneath: under the bed, under the rain.

examples.tr: The cat is under the bed.
The bag is under the table.
We are walking in (lit. under) the rain.

etymology.text: Adverbial accusative of تَحْت (taḥt, “the place below”); related to Hebrew תַּחַת (táḥat) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew תַּחַת (tachat) is the same word — and in Hebrew it can also mean “instead of”.
pitfalls: تَحْتَ ends in -a (an old accusative) and the noun after it is genitive: تَحْتَ الطَّاوِلَةِ.
Alone, as an adverb, it is تَحْتُ (taḥtu): مِنْ تَحْتُ (from below).
subtleties: Figurative uses: تَحْتَ الْمُرَاقَبَةِ (under observation), تَحْتَ الطَّلَبِ (on request).

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses بِجَانِبِ as “along, side by side with” (from جَانِب, “side”), i.e. next to, beside.

profile.feeling: Side by side: next to.

senses.def: in addition to, apart from (usually إِلَى جَانِبِ)

examples.tr: The lamp is next to the bed.
The pharmacy is next to the bank.
Sit next to me.

synonyms.nuance: beside — the same word without بِ

etymology.text: From بِـ (bi-, “at, on”) + جَانِب (jānib, “side”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: جَانِب (side) belongs to the root ج ن ب, which also gives أَجْنَبِيّ, “foreigner” — someone from the side, an outsider.
pitfalls: One written word with بِ: بِجَانِبِ — and it ends in -i (the genitive after بِ), not *bi-jāniba.
The noun after it is genitive too: بِجَانِبِ الْبَابِ.
subtleties: إِلَى جَانِبِ also means “in addition to”: إِلَى جَانِبِ عَمَلِهِ يَدْرُسُ (besides his work, he studies).

profile.feeling: Facing it: in front of, ahead.

senses.def: in the presence of; in the face of

examples.tr: The car is in front of the house.
I’ll wait for you in front of the school.
A long day lies ahead of us.

synonyms.nuance: in front of (spoken ʾuddām / ʾiddām in Egypt and the Levant)

etymology.text: The accusative of the noun أَمَام (“front, the place before something”) used as a preposition (Wiktionary gives both).

funFacts: إِمَام (imam, “the one in front”, who leads the prayer) and أُمَّة (nation) share its root ء م م.
pitfalls: أَمَامَ (ʾamāma, in front of) vs إِمَام (ʾimām, prayer leader): watch the first vowel.
subtleties: It works for time too: أَمَامَنَا يَوْمٌ طَوِيلٌ (a long day lies ahead of us).

profile.feeling: At the back: behind.

examples.tr: The garden is behind the house.
Who is behind the door?
Look behind you!

synonyms.nuance: behind — also figurative: the reason behind, beyond

etymology.text: The accusative of the noun خَلْف (“the place behind; the back; successor”), root خ ل ف, used as a preposition (Wiktionary).

funFacts: خَلِيفَة (caliph) is “the one who comes after = the successor”, from the same root.
pitfalls: خ (ḫ, the ch of German Bach), not ح: ḫalfa.
subtleties: خَلْفَ is concrete (physically behind); وَرَاءَ can also be figurative: مَا وَرَاءَ الْخَبَرِ (what is behind the news).

profile.feeling: Behind and beyond — what is hidden.

examples.tr: The kitchen is behind this door.
The sun is behind the mountain.
What is the secret behind his success?

phrases.tr: behind every great man there is a woman
phrases.meaning: a man’s success often owes much to a woman’s support

etymology.text: Wiktionary, after Lane’s Lexicon: from the root و ر ء or و ر ي, “to push back behind something, to cover over”.

funFacts: مَا وَرَاءَ الطَّبِيعَةِ, “what is beyond nature”, is the Arabic for metaphysics — exactly Greek μετὰ τὰ φυσικά.
pitfalls: With pronoun endings the hamza changes its seat: وَرَائِي (behind me), but وَرَاءَكَ, وَرَاءَهُ.
It starts with و, but it is not the prefix “and”: وَرَاءَ is one word.
subtleties: وَرَاءَ often sounds a little more literary than خَلْفَ.

profile.feeling: In the middle of two: between.

examples.tr: The bank is between the restaurant and the pharmacy.
There is a street between the house and the school.
This is a secret between you and me.

etymology.text: Wiktionary compares Hebrew בֵּין (bein), Aramaic byn, Ugaritic bn, Geʿez bäynä and Old South Arabian byn; synchronically an adverbial accusative of بَيْن (“interval”), root ب ي ن.

funFacts: Hebrew בֵּין (bein) is the same word, and both languages repeat it with pronouns: بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ — בֵּינִי לְבֵינְךָ.
pitfalls: With pronoun endings بَيْنَ is repeated: بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ (between me and you); with two nouns once is enough: بَيْنَ الْبَيْتِ وَالْمَدْرَسَةِ.
بَيْنَ (between) ends in n — not بَيْت (house).
subtleties: بَيْنَمَا (while) is built on it (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: Close by, within reach — also close to the heart.

examples.tr: The bank is near here.
The school is close to home.
Is the airport close?
He is a close friend.

synonyms.nuance: near, in the vicinity of — a place phrase

etymology.text: A faʿīl-type stative adjective from قَرُبَ (qaruba, “to be near”); cognate with Hebrew קָרוֹב (karóv, “close, near”) and Amharic ቅርብ (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew קָרוֹב (karov) is “near” and “a relative” too — exactly like Arabic قَرِيب (near; a relative, lesson 6).
pitfalls: It agrees like an adjective: الْبَنْكُ قَرِيبٌ, but الْمَدْرَسَةُ قَرِيبَةٌ.
“Near something” takes مِنْ: قَرِيبٌ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ.
subtleties: The same word is the noun “relative” (lesson 6), with the plurals أَقَارِبُ / أَقْرِبَاءُ; as “near” its plural is قَرِيبُونَ.
Wiktionary: the feminine can also be قَرِيب, as in the Qurʾān: إِنَّ رَحْمَتَ اللّٰهِ قَرِيبٌ (7:56).

profile.feeling: Distance — and unlikeliness.

examples.tr: My house is far from work.
The village is very far.
That is unlikely.

etymology.text: A faʿīl-type stative adjective from بَعُدَ (baʕuda, “to be far”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: بَعْدَ (after) and بُعْد (distance) belong to the same root ب ع د.
pitfalls: “Far from” is بَعِيدٌ عَنْ — or بَعِيدٌ مِنْ; عَنْ is more common.
It agrees: الْقَرْيَةُ بَعِيدَةٌ (f.).
subtleties: لَيْسَ بَعِيدًا = it is not far; مِنْ بَعِيدٍ = from afar.

profile.feeling: Indoors, within — the inside of things.

senses.def: inside — دَاخِلَ + a noun (inside the house), فِي الدَّاخِلِ (inside, indoors)
the inside, the interior; (of a country) the interior, home

examples.tr: The children are inside.
The key is inside the bag.
Shall we sit inside the restaurant or outside?
The inside of the house is beautiful.

synonyms.nuance: inside (spoken juwwa, Egypt and the Levant)

etymology.text: Derived from the active participle of دَخَلَ (daḫala, “to enter, to go in”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Signs say دُخُول (entrance) and خُرُوج (exit) — the verbal nouns of دَخَلَ and خَرَجَ, the verbs behind دَاخِل and خَارِج.
pitfalls: دَاخِلَ (with -a, + genitive) = inside something: دَاخِلَ الْبَيْتِ. Without an object say فِي الدَّاخِلِ.
It is a noun: the case shows on it — دَاخِلُ الْبَيْتِ (the inside of the house) is a subject.
subtleties: دَاخِلِيّ = internal, domestic: وَزَارَةُ الدَّاخِلِيَّةِ (the Ministry of the Interior).

profile.feeling: Out of doors — and abroad.

senses.def: outside — خَارِجَ + a noun (outside the house), فِي الْخَارِجِ (outside, out of doors)

examples.tr: The children are playing outside.
The car is outside the house.
My brother works abroad.

etymology.text: Derived from the active participle of the verb خَرَجَ (ḫaraja, “to go out”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The verbal noun خُرُوج is the “Exit” sign; the Kharijites (الْخَوَارِجُ), “those who went out”, are named after the same verb.
pitfalls: فِي الْخَارِجِ is “outside” or “abroad” — the context decides.
خَارِجَ + genitive: خَارِجَ الْبَيْتِ.
subtleties: خَارِجِيّ = external, foreign: وَزِيرُ الْخَارِجِيَّةِ (foreign minister).

profile.feeling: Directions in the street: turn left.

senses.def: left (side): عَلَى الْيَسَارِ (on the left), إِلَى الْيَسَارِ (to the left)

examples.tr: The bank is on the left.
Look to the left.
The kitchen is to the left of the door.
left-wing parties

synonyms.nuance: left — the spoken word in Egypt and the Levant (šmāl); in Standard Arabic شِمَال is “north”

etymology.text: Root ي س ر (y s r, “ease”); Wiktionary relates it to أَيْسَر (“left; easier”) and gives no further etymology.

funFacts: Arabic is written مِنَ الْيَمِينِ إِلَى الْيَسَارِ — from right to left.
pitfalls: In the Levant and Egypt “left” is شْمَال — the Standard word for “north”: do not get lost!
For a hand or a side Arabic often uses the adjective: الْيَدُ الْيُسْرَى (the left hand).
subtleties: With a noun or pronoun: عَلَى يَسَارِ الْبَابِ (to the left of the door), عَلَى يَسَارِكَ (on your left).

profile.feeling: Directions — and the right hand of oaths.

senses.def: right (side): عَلَى الْيَمِينِ (on the right), إِلَى الْيَمِينِ (to the right)

examples.tr: The pharmacy is on the right.
Go right.
He took the oath before the judge.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym for the side; for a hand or a side Arabic uses the adjective: الْيَدُ الْيُمْنَى (the right hand), الْجَانِبُ الْأَيْمَنُ (the right side).

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *yamīn- (“right”), from Proto-Afroasiatic *yamin- (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew יָמִין (yamin) is the same word, and Benjamin, בִּנְיָמִין, is “son of the right hand”.
pitfalls: يَمِين is also “oath” (feminine, plural أَيْمَان): حَلَفَ الْيَمِينَ = he took the oath.
Wiktionary gives it as masculine or feminine; as a direction you will rarely need its gender.
subtleties: On your right: عَلَى يَمِينِكَ; the right side: الْجِهَةُ الْيُمْنَى.

profile.feeling: Smells of cooking: the heart of the home.

examples.tr: My mother is in the kitchen.
The fridge is in the kitchen.
I love Lebanese cooking.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: مَطْبَخ is the kitchen everywhere in the Arab world.

etymology.text: Noun of place from the verb طَبَخَ (ṭabaḫa, “to cook”), root ط ب خ; compare Hebrew מִטְבָּח (mitbaḥ) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish mutfak and Hebrew מִטְבָּח (mitbach) are the same word: “the place of cooking”.
pitfalls: ط and خ: maṭbaḫ — two sounds that Greek and German do not have.
The plural مَطَابِخُ is a diptote.
subtleties: Like English “kitchen” and German Küche, مَطْبَخ is also a cuisine: الْمَطْبَخُ الْمَغْرِبِيُّ (Moroccan cooking).

profile.feeling: Bathroom, toilet — and the steam of the hammam.

examples.tr: The bathroom is on the right.
Where is the toilet, please?
We went to the Turkish bath.

etymology.text: From the root ح م م (ḥ m m), related to heating (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English hammam and Turkish hamam are this word: “the heating place”, the steam bath.
pitfalls: حَمَّام (ḥammām, bathroom) has a doubled m; حَمَام (ḥamām) is “pigeons”.
subtleties: “Where is the toilet?” is simply أَيْنَ الْحَمَّامُ؟ — حَمَّام covers bathroom and WC.

profile.feeling: Sleep, rest and privacy.

senses.def: bedroom — غُرْفَةُ النَّوْمِ (the bedroom), غُرْفَةُ نَوْمٍ (a bedroom)

examples.tr: The bedroom is big.
I’m in the bedroom.
The flat has one bedroom.

synonyms.nuance: room — at home often simply غُرْفَتِي, my room

etymology.text: غُرْفَة (room) + نَوْم (sleep, the verbal noun of نَامَ, “to sleep”): “a room of sleep”. Wiktionary lists the compound.

funFacts: Arabic builds such words with a construct, where German writes one word: غُرْفَةُ نَوْمٍ = Schlafzimmer, غُرْفَةُ جُلُوسٍ = Wohnzimmer.
pitfalls: Only the second word takes the article: غُرْفَةُ النَّوْمِ (the bedroom); the case ending is on the first: فِي غُرْفَةِ النَّوْمِ.
In the plural only the first word changes: غُرَفُ نَوْمٍ.
subtleties: The tāʾ marbūṭa is pronounced -t in the construct: ġurfat an-nawm.

profile.feeling: Tea with guests, television and the family sofa.

senses.def: living room, sitting room — غُرْفَةُ الْجُلُوسِ (the living room)

examples.tr: We drink tea in the living room.
The sofa is in the living room.
The living room is spacious.

synonyms.nuance: living room, hall — common in the Levant and the Gulf; also a hall: صَالَةُ الرِّيَاضَةِ (gym)
salon, reception room for guests (from French salon)
living room — a calque of English “living room”

etymology.text: غُرْفَة (room) + جُلُوس (sitting, the verbal noun of جَلَسَ, “to sit”): “the sitting room”. Wiktionary has no entry for the compound; its synonym صَالَة is from Italian sala.

funFacts: صَالَة comes from Italian sala (Wiktionary), the same Germanic word as German Saal.
pitfalls: Like غُرْفَةُ نَوْمٍ: the article goes on the second word only — غُرْفَةُ الْجُلُوسِ.
subtleties: Many homes have both: a صَالُون for guests and a غُرْفَةُ جُلُوسٍ or صَالَة for the family.

profile.feeling: Tiles, wood and the surface under your feet.

examples.tr: The floor is clean.
The books are on the floor.
My room has a wooden floor.

synonyms.nuance: ground, earth — “on the floor” is usually عَلَى الْأَرْضِ

etymology.text: From أَرْض (ʔarḍ, “earth, ground”) + ـِيَّة (-iyya) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: أَرْض (earth) is Hebrew אֶרֶץ (erets): the same Semitic word.
pitfalls: A floor = storey of a building is طَابِق, not أَرْضِيَّة.
subtleties: عَلَى الْأَرْضِ (on the ground / floor) is the everyday phrase; أَرْضِيَّة names the surface itself (tiles, wood, cleaning).

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses دَرَج as “staircase, ladder” — the stairs of the concept; the check does not find “stairs” inside “staircase”.

profile.feeling: Up and down: the staircase.

examples.tr: The stairs are in front of the door.
I go up the stairs to my room.
Don’t sit on the stairs.

synonyms.nuance: steps — the plural of دَرَجَة, one step

etymology.text: Wiktionary compares Geʿez dərgät, Hebrew דֶּרֶג (dereg), Classical Syriac and Aramaic dargā.

funFacts: دَرَجَة (one step) also means “degree” and “class”: دَرَجَةٌ أُولَى (first class), عِشْرُونَ دَرَجَةً (twenty degrees).
pitfalls: دَرَج (daraj, stairs) vs دُرْج (durj, drawer): only the vowels differ.
“The stairs” is a singular in Arabic: الدَّرَجُ طَوِيلٌ (the stairs are long).
subtleties: Wiktionary gives the plurals أَدْرَاج and دِرَاج; in practice one says الدَّرَجُ for one staircase and counts the steps (دَرَجَات).

profile.feeling: Books, jars and things put away.

examples.tr: The books are on the shelf.
Put the cup on the shelf.
The library has many shelves.

phrases.tr: he put it on the shelf
phrases.meaning: he shelved it, set it aside

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym; a whole bookcase is مَكْتَبَة or خِزَانَةُ كُتُبٍ.

etymology.text: Disputed (Wiktionary): native, from the root ر ف ف (an outstretched wing, a cover), or from Aramaic rap (“level, storey”).

funFacts: Wiktionary records several theories — one sees in it a cloth stretched over a window like a wing.
pitfalls: The f is doubled: رَفّ (raff); الرَّفُّ, عَلَى الرَّفِّ. Plural رُفُوف (also أَرْفُف).
subtleties: عَلَى الرَّفِّ can mean “shelved, put aside” — a project or a law.

profile.feeling: Comfort at home: the family sofa.

examples.tr: The sofa is in the living room.
The cat is asleep on the sofa.
We bought a new sofa.

synonyms.nuance: sofa, couch — the classical word (also “throne” in the Qurʾān)

etymology.text: Not an entry in Wiktionary’s Arabic data; it matches Turkish kanepe, which Wiktionary derives from French canapé — itself, through Latin cōnōpēum, from Ancient Greek κωνωπεῖον (“a couch with a mosquito net”).

funFacts: The chain begins in Greek: κωνωπεῖον was a couch with a net against mosquitoes (κώνωψ, “mosquito”); Modern Greek καναπές and κουνούπι are its descendants (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Not a classical word: in formal writing you will also see أَرِيكَة.
subtleties: Feminine in ة: الْكَنَبَةُ مُرِيحَةٌ; plural كَنَبَات.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses ثَلَّاجَة as “refrigerator”, i.e. the fridge.

profile.feeling: Cold drinks on a hot day.

examples.tr: The milk is in the fridge.
The fridge is empty!
Put the cheese in the fridge.

etymology.text: Tool noun from the root ث ل ج (ṯ l j, “snow, ice”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: ثَلْج is snow and ice; Hebrew שֶׁלֶג (sheleg, snow) is its cousin.
pitfalls: ث is the th of English “think”, and the l is doubled: ṯallāja.
subtleties: faʿʿāla is a pattern for machines: ثَلَّاجَة (fridge), غَسَّالَة (washing machine), سَيَّارَة (car).
